lesson.title: Keeping Every Clock on the Internet Honest
lesson.summary: NTP is the application layer protocol that keeps computers' clocks synchronized across the internet using a hierarchical system of time sources called strata.
lesson.body:
Every computer has its own internal clock, and left alone, those clocks drift. A cheap crystal oscillator can gain or lose several seconds a day, and over weeks that error compounds into minutes. For a single laptop checking the time to display in a corner of the screen, that barely matters. But the internet is full of systems that depend on many machines agreeing, closely, on what time it is right now: logs from different servers need timestamps that can be compared to reconstruct what happened during an outage, distributed databases need to order events correctly, and, as you will see later in this unit, security certificates carry a validity window that only makes sense if the machine checking it has a roughly accurate clock. The Network Time Protocol, NTP, exists to solve this quietly and continuously in the background.

NTP is an application layer protocol, meaning it defines a message format and a set of rules that ride on top of the transport layer, in this case using UDP on port 123. What makes NTP interesting is not the message format itself but the hierarchy it uses to distribute accurate time without overwhelming the most authoritative sources. NTP organizes time servers into strata. Stratum 0 refers to reference clocks themselves, devices like atomic clocks or GPS receivers, which are extremely accurate but are not directly part of the network. Stratum 1 servers are machines directly connected to a stratum 0 device, so they can serve highly accurate time to others. Stratum 2 servers synchronize from stratum 1 servers, stratum 3 servers synchronize from stratum 2, and so on, down through a defined maximum. Each hop away from stratum 0 introduces a small amount of additional uncertainty, but the tree structure means a single atomic clock can, indirectly, help keep millions of ordinary machines in sync without being contacted directly by any of them.

The synchronization itself is more careful than just asking a server what time it is and copying the answer, because the request and response take time to travel across the network, and that travel time would otherwise get baked in as error. NTP handles this with four timestamps. The client records the time it sent its request. The server records the time it received that request and the time it sent its reply. The client records the time it received the reply. With those four values, NTP can estimate both the round trip network delay and the offset between the two clocks, and adjust the local clock accordingly rather than just overwriting it with whatever the server reported.

In practice, an ordinary laptop typically does not talk to a stratum 1 server directly. It might query a pool of public NTP servers, which themselves are often stratum 2, already synchronized to stratum 1 machines that are wired to GPS receivers or atomic clocks. The laptop never needs to know or care about that chain, it just ends up with a clock accurate to a small fraction of a second, which is exactly the kind of invisible infrastructure that later chapters in this unit will turn out to depend on.
